cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XX
The night before;\nthe omens of the last day; the ox-hoof; Theoclymenus sees the dark.
But noble Odysseus made his bed in the fore-hall:
he spread an undressed oxhide down, and over it many\nfleeces of the sheep the Achaeans kept slaughtering,
and Eurynome threw a mantle over him where he lay.
There Odysseus lay awake, his heart devising evils\nfor the suitors; and out of the hall came the women,
the ones who all along had been sleeping with the suitors,
setting each other laughing, trading their good cheer.
And the heart was roused in his breast,\nand he weighed it long in his mind and in his heart —
whether to spring after them and deal out death to each,\nor let them mix with the overweening suitors
one final and last time. And the heart inside him snarled —\nas a bitch standing over her soft-boned pups,
facing a man she does not know,\nsnarls and is wild to fight:
so his heart snarled within him,\nin outrage at their evil doings.
But he struck his chest and called his heart to order:
"Bear up, my heart.\nA more dog-vile thing you bore than this
the day the Cyclops, his force past holding,\nate my brave companions — and you endured it, till cunning
led you out of the cave where you thought to die."
So he spoke, reproving the dear heart in his breast;\nand his heart, in deep obedience, held fast
and endured without a break. But the\nman himself turned this way and that.
As when a man before a great blazing fire\nturns a paunch packed full of fat and blood
this way and that, longing to have it roasted quickly,\nso he rolled from side to side, turning over
how he could lay his hands on the shameless suitors,\none man against so many. And Athena came close to him,
down from the sky; and in body she was like a woman;\nand she stood above his head and spoke to him:
"Why awake again, most luckless of all men?
Here is your house; here in the house is your wife,\nand your child — a son such as any man would pray for."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Yes, goddess — all this you have said as it should be.
But there is a thing my heart keeps turning over:
how I am to lay hands on the shameless suitors — I,\none man alone; and they always inside in a crowd.
And this greater thing besides I keep turning over:
even if I kill them, by the will of Zeus and by yours,
where do I run from what follows?\nThink that out for me, I say."
Then the goddess answered him, gray-eyed Athena:
"Hard man! A person will trust a weaker friend than me,\none who is mortal, and does not know such counsels;
but I am a god, and I guard you through to the\nend of every labor. I will tell you outright:
if fifty companies of mortal men stood round\nthe two of us, hot to kill us in the fight,
even so you would drive away their cattle and fat sheep.
Come — let sleep take you too. There is misery in watching
all night awake. You will rise up out of your evils now."
So she spoke, and poured down sleep upon his eyelids,\nand went back herself to Olympus, the shining goddess.
And as sleep seized him, loosing the cares of his heart,\nloosing his limbs, his true-hearted wife awoke,
and wept, sitting up on her soft bed.
And when she had had her fill of weeping,\nfirst to Artemis prayed that woman shining among women:
"Artemis, sovereign goddess,\ndaughter of Zeus — would that now
you would plant an arrow in my breast and take my\nlife this very instant — or a storm-wind snatch me up
and carry me off down the ways of gloom and fling\nme down where backward-flowing Ocean empties.
As when the storm-winds carried off Pandareus' daughters:
the gods had destroyed their parents, and they were left
orphans in the halls; and shining Aphrodite reared\nthem on cheese and sweet honey and pleasant wine,
and Hera gave them beauty and good sense beyond\nall women, and pure Artemis their height,
and Athena taught them the making of glorious work.
But while shining Aphrodite was on her way to high Olympus
to ask for the girls the crown of blossoming marriage —
gone to Zeus who delights in thunder,\nfor he knows all things well,
the fortune and the misfortune of mortal men —\nmeanwhile the snatching-winds carried the girls away
and gave them over to the hateful Furies, to serve them.
So may the dwellers on Olympus blot me out of sight,\nor fair-braided Artemis strike me, that with Odysseus
before my eyes I may pass even under the hateful earth,\nand never gladden the mind of a lesser man.
And yet an evil is bearable, when a person weeps through\nthe days, grieved to the packed core of the heart,
and the nights hold sleep at least —\nfor sleep makes one forget
everything, the good and the bad,\nonce it has wrapped the eyelids —
but to me the god sends evil even in dreams.
For this very night one slept beside me — like him,
his very likeness as he was when\nhe went with the army; and my heart
rejoiced: I thought it no dream,\nbut the waking truth at last."
So she spoke; and at once Dawn\nof the golden throne came on.
And noble Odysseus caught the sound of her weeping,
and mused; and it seemed to him,\nin the drift of his heart,
that she knew him already, and stood beside his head.
He gathered up the mantle and the fleeces he had slept\nin and set them on a chair in the hall; the oxhide
he carried outside and laid down;\nand lifting his hands he prayed to Zeus:
"Father Zeus — if you gods willed it, and brought me home
over dry land and water, after all your hard usage,\nlet someone of the people waking in the house speak me
a word of omen; and outside,\nlet another sign of Zeus appear."
So he prayed; and Zeus the counselor heard him,\nand at once he thundered out of gleaming Olympus,
down from on high, out of the clouds.\nAnd noble Odysseus was glad.
And the word of omen came from\na woman grinding at the mill,
close by, where the mills of the\nshepherd of the people stood.
Twelve women in all kept them turning,\nmaking barley meal and wheat flour, the marrow of men.
The others were asleep, their wheat all ground;\nonly one had not finished — the frailest one of all.
She stopped her stone now,\nand spoke the word — a sign for her master:
"Father Zeus, you who rule the gods and mankind:
how loud you thundered out of the starry sky —\nand no cloud anywhere! You show this as a sign to someone.
Then accomplish now for wretched me the word I say:
may the suitors, on this day,\nfor the last and latest time,
take up their lovely feasting in the halls of Odysseus —
the men who have loosed my knees with heart-grinding labor
as I make their barley meal: may they sup now their last!"
So she spoke; and noble Odysseus\nrejoiced at the omen of her word
and at the thunder of Zeus.\nHe told himself the guilty would pay.
Now the other slave-women, gathering\nin the beautiful house of Odysseus,
were kindling on the hearth the never-wearying fire.
And Telemachus rose from his bed, a man like a god,
and put on his clothes, and hung\nhis sharp sword at his shoulder,
and under his shining feet he bound the beautiful sandals,
and took his strong spear, tipped with sharpened bronze,\nand paused on the threshold, and said to Eurycleia:
"Dear nurse, have you honored the stranger in our house
with bed and food? Or does he lie untended, as he may?
That is my mother's way — sensible woman though she is:
she honors the worse of mortal men on impulse,\nand sends the better man away unhonored."
Then watchful-minded Eurycleia answered him:
"Child, do not blame the blameless woman now.
He sat and drank his wine as long as he himself would;
and bread — he said he hungered for none: she asked him.
And when he began to think of rest and sleep,\nshe told the slave-women to spread him a proper bed;
but he — like a man wholly wretched, out of luck —\nrefused to sleep on a bedstead under blankets:
on an undressed oxhide and the fleeces of sheep
he slept in the fore-hall.\nWe laid a mantle over him ourselves."
So she spoke; and Telemachus went out through the hall,\nspear in hand; two swift dogs followed with him,
and he went to the assembly-place,\nto the strong-greaved Achaeans.
And she called out to the slave-women,\nthat woman shining among women —
Eurycleia, daughter of Ops, Peisenor's son:
"Come — to work! Some of you sweep the house, and briskly,\nand sprinkle it, and lay the crimson coverings
on the well-made chairs; others take sponges and\nwipe down all the tables, and rinse the mixing-bowls
and the wrought double-handled cups;\nand the rest of you away
for water at the spring —\ngo quick, and quick back with it.
The suitors will not be long out of the hall this morning:
they will come very early.\nIt is festival for everyone today."
So she spoke; and they listened well and obeyed:
twenty went off to the spring of dark water,\nand the others worked away skillfully about the house.
Then the Achaeans' serving-men came in, and split firewood,\nwell and skillfully; and the women came back
from the spring; and after them came the swineherd,\ndriving three fatted hogs, the best of all he had.
He left them to feed at large in the fine yard-fences,
and himself spoke to Odysseus, and his words were kind:
"Stranger — do the Achaeans look on you any better now,
or do they still dishonor you\nthrough the hall, as before?"
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Ah, Eumaeus, may the gods pay back the outrage\nthese men in their insolence keep devising —
reckless things, in another man's house.\nThey have no share of shame."
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And Melanthius came up close to them, the goatherd,\ndriving the goats that stood out in all the herds,
a dinner for the suitors;\nand two herdsmen followed with him.
He tethered the goats under the echoing porch,\nand himself spoke to Odysseus, and his words were taunts:
"Stranger — still here? Still going to plague this house,\nbegging from the men? Still not out the door?
I don't imagine, now, we two will settle this business
before we've tasted each other's\nfists. There is no decency
in the way you beg. And there are\nother feasts among the Achaeans."
So he spoke; and Odysseus of\nthe many designs said nothing:
he only shook his head, silent,\nbrooding evils deep in his heart.
And a third came in upon them —\nPhiloetius, a leader of men,
driving a barren heifer for the suitors, and fat goats.
Ferrymen had brought them over — the ones who\ncarry other travelers too, whoever comes to them.
He tethered his beasts well under the echoing porch,\nand came up close to the swineherd and asked him:
"Swineherd — who is this stranger, newly come to\nour house? What men does he claim for his people?
Where are his family and his fathers' fields?
Poor devil — and yet, truly,\nin build he is like a lord, a king.
But the gods sink far-wandering men in misery\nwhen they spin hard sorrow even for kings."
He spoke, and coming up he gave him his right hand in\nwelcome, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words:
"Your health, father stranger! May happiness be yours
in time to come — though now\nyou are held fast in many evils.
Father Zeus — no other god is deadlier than you:
you have no pity on men, though you begot them yourself,\nfor tangling them in misery and grinding pains.
I broke sweat when I saw him, and my eyes stand full\nof tears, remembering Odysseus: for he too, I think,
wears rags like these, and wanders somewhere among men —\nif indeed he lives, and sees the light of the sun.
But if he is dead already, down in the house of Hades —
ah me, blameless Odysseus! — who set me over his cattle
when I was still a boy, in the land of the Cephallenians.
And now they are past all counting: no other man
could have a breed of broad-browed\ncattle bear richer, like standing wheat.
And strangers order me to drive them in for them to eat!\nThey care nothing for the son in the house,
they do not tremble at the gods'\nwatching eye: they are wild
to divide up the goods of the master so long away.
As for me, this thought keeps rolling over and over\nin the heart in my breast: it is a very bad thing,
while the son lives, to go off to a country of strangers,
cattle and all, to foreign men; but colder still to stay
suffering here, sitting over cattle that others claim.
And long ago I would have run, fled to some other of\nthe high-handed kings — for this is past all bearing —
but still I think of that unlucky man: what if he came
from somewhere, and made a scattering\nof the suitors through the house!"
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Cowherd — since you seem no bad man and no fool,
and I can see for myself that\ngood sense has reached your heart,
I will tell you something, and swear a great oath upon it:
Now Zeus be my witness, first of the gods,\nand this table of friendship,
and the hearth of blameless Odysseus,\nto which I have come:
while you are here, Odysseus will come home;\nand with your own eyes, if you wish it, you shall see
the killing of the suitors who play lord and master here."
Then the cowherd answered him, the master of the oxen:
"Ah, stranger, if only the son of\nCronos would accomplish that word!
Then you would learn my strength —\nand how my hands follow it."
And in the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods
that Odysseus of the many designs\nmight come home to his own house.
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And the suitors, meanwhile, were framing death and doom
for Telemachus — when a bird came by on their left hand:
an eagle flying high, gripping a trembling dove.
And Amphinomus rose and spoke among them:
"Friends, this plan of ours will not run smooth —\nthe killing of Telemachus. Let us think of the feast."
So spoke Amphinomus, and his word pleased them well.
They came into the house of godlike Odysseus and\nlaid their mantles down on the couches and chairs
and slaughtered big sheep and fat goats,\nslaughtered sleek hogs and a heifer of the herd.
They roasted the innards and served them round, and mixed
the wine in the mixing-bowls;\nand the swineherd passed the cups,
and Philoetius, a leader of men, passed them bread\nin beautiful baskets; and Melanthius poured the wine.
And their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But Telemachus — his craft at work — seated Odysseus
inside the strong-built hall, beside the stone threshold,\nsetting him a battered stool and a little table;
he put a portion of the innards by him,\nand poured him wine in a golden cup, and said to him:
"Sit here now among the men, and drink your wine.
The taunts and the fists of all the suitors —\nI myself will hold them off you. This is no public house:
it is Odysseus' house — and he won it for me.
And you, you suitors, hold your hearts back from insult\nand fists, so no strife and quarreling break out."
So he spoke; and they all bit their lips and stared\nin wonder at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
And Antinous spoke among them, Eupeithes' son:
"Hard as it is, Achaeans, let us take the word of\nTelemachus — though how he threatens as he talks!
Zeus the son of Cronos would not have it; otherwise
we would have silenced him in the\nhalls long since — so clear a speaker."
So spoke Antinous; but he took no heed of his words.
Now the heralds were leading\nthrough the town the holy hecatomb
of the gods; and the long-haired Achaeans gathered\nunder the shady grove of Apollo who shoots from afar.
And when they had roasted the\nouter flesh and drawn it off,
they divided the portions and feasted the glorious feast;\nand the serving-men set beside Odysseus a share
equal to the ones they drew themselves:\nfor so ordered Telemachus, dear son of godlike Odysseus.
And Athena would not let the lordly suitors hold back\nfrom heart-stinging outrage — so that pain might sink
still deeper into Laertes' son Odysseus.
There was among the suitors a man versed in lawlessness:
Ctesippus was his name, and his home was on Same;\nsure of his fabulous wealth, he had come
to woo the wife of Odysseus, the master so long away.
He now spoke out among the overweening suitors:
"Hear me, you lordly suitors, while I say a word.
The stranger has long had his portion — an equal one,
as is proper: it is not fine, and it is not just, to stint
the guests of Telemachus, whoever comes to this house.
But come — let me too give him a guest-gift, so he in turn
can hand a prize to the bath-woman, or to some other\nof the slaves in the house of godlike Odysseus."
So speaking, he snatched an ox-hoof out of the basket
where it lay, and hurled it with\nhis thick hand. But Odysseus
dodged it with a quick tilt of\nhis head, and smiled in his heart
a smile most sardonic; and it struck the well-built wall.
And Telemachus lashed Ctesippus with his words:
"Ctesippus — count it clear profit for your own heart:
you missed the stranger. He dodged the throw himself.
Otherwise I would have run you through\nthe middle with my sharp spear,
and instead of a wedding your father would be busy\nhere with a funeral. So: let no man show his ugliness
in this house of mine. For now I\ntake note and I know each thing,
the good and the worse alike. Before, I was still a child.
But even so we endure it and look on:
the flocks slaughtered, the wine drunk down,\nthe bread — for it is hard for one man to check many.
Come then, do me no more evil in your malice.
But if you are set on killing me —\nme myself — with the bronze,
even that I would choose: it would be far better to\ndie than look on forever at these disgraceful doings:
guests roughly handled, and men hauling the\nslave-women shamefully through the beautiful house."
So he spoke; and they all fell silent and still.
At last Agelaus spoke, Damastor's son:
"Friends — no man should take offense at a just word\nspoken, and answer it with wrangling and hard speech.
Do not knock the stranger about, nor any other\nof the slaves in the house of godlike Odysseus.
But to Telemachus, and to his mother, I would say
a gentle word — if it might find\nfavor with the hearts of both.
As long as the hearts in your breasts kept hope
that Odysseus of the many designs\nwould come home to his own house,
no one could resent your waiting, or your holding\noff the suitors in the halls: that was the better way
if Odysseus had returned, come back at last to his house.
But now it is plain that he is past returning.
Go then, sit by your mother, and lay it out for her:
marry the best man, the one who offers most —\nso you may keep and enjoy all that was your father's,
eating and drinking, and she may keep another's house."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"No, by Zeus, Agelaus —\nand by the sufferings of my father,
who far from Ithaca has perished, or still wanders:
I do not delay my mother's marriage. I urge her to wed\nthe man she chooses; and I offer gifts past counting.
But I am ashamed to drive her\nfrom the hall against her will
with a word of compulsion.\nMay god never bring that to pass."
So spoke Telemachus. And in the suitors Pallas Athena
set off unquenchable laughter,\nand knocked their wits askew.
And now they were laughing with jaws no longer their own;
the meat they ate was dabbled in blood; and their eyes
brimmed full of tears;\nand the heart in them wanted to wail.
And godlike Theoclymenus spoke out among them:
"Wretched men — what evil is this\nyou suffer? Night — your heads
are shrouded in night, and your\nfaces, and your knees beneath;
wailing has caught like fire; cheeks are streaming tears;
the walls are spattered with blood,\nand the fine crossbeams;
and the porch is full of ghosts —\nthe courtyard full of them —
ghosts hurrying down to Erebus, under the gloom; the sun
has perished out of the sky,\nand an evil mist runs over everything."
So he spoke; and they all laughed at him sweetly.
And Eurymachus, Polybus' son, began to speak among them:
"The stranger is raving — this new one, fresh from abroad.
Quick, young men — see him out of the house and on his way
to the assembly-place, since he finds it night in here."
Then godlike Theoclymenus said to him:
"Eurymachus, I ask no escort of you for my going.
I have eyes, and ears, and both my feet,\nand a mind in my breast in no way meanly made.
With these I am going out that door — for I see evil\ncoming on you, evil no man will escape or dodge,
no man of you suitors, you who\nin the house of godlike Odysseus
batter men with outrage and devise your reckless deeds."
So speaking he went out of the well-settled house\nand came to Piraeus, who received him gladly.
And the suitors all, eyeing one another, went to\nwork needling Telemachus, laughing at his guests;
and a man of the arrogant young men would say:
"Telemachus, no man is unluckier in his guests than you.
Look at this one you keep — this pawed-over vagrant\nwho wants his bread and wine, who has no skill for work
and no strength either: a dead weight on the good earth.
And then the other one — he stood up to play the prophet!
If you would listen to me, the profit is all yours:
let us pitch your guests into a many-benched ship
and send them to the Sicilians.\nThere they would fetch you a worthy price."
So the suitors talked; but he took no heed of their words.
He watched his father in silence — waiting, always,
for the moment he would lay his\nhands on the shameless suitors.
And she — she had set her\nbeautiful chair across from them:
Icarius' daughter, watchful-minded Penelope,\nand heard each man's word in the halls.
For laughing they had made their dinner ready —
a sweet meal and a hearty one,\nfor they had slaughtered lavishly.
But no supper could ever be more graceless than the\nsupper a goddess and a strong man were soon now to set
before them. For they had begun it:\nthe shameful devising was theirs.
